parts.title: Plants, seasons and soil in Rawdhat Khuraym, Saudi Arabia: a plant-rich oasis in one of the driest places on Earth
parts.abstract:
In dry regions, a rawdah is a natural hollow where rainwater collects. These places have their own special plants and wildlife. They help animals survive, soften the effects of the climate, and give people and nature many other benefits. To look after a rawdah well, we first need to know which plants grow there and how they change over time.

Rawdhat Khuraym is a plant-rich area in the Riyadh region of Saudi Arabia. It has recently become part of the Imam Abdulaziz bin Mohammed Royal Reserve. For 23 years, nobody had studied which plants grow in this rawdah, even though it matters both to local culture and to nature. We wanted to help people protect it and restore it well, so we set out to do five things:

(1) update the list of plants growing in Rawdhat Khuraym in the dry and wet seasons;
(2) find the main plant communities in each separate part of Rawdhat Khuraym;
(3) find which soil features control the different plant communities;
(4) judge how much the reserve's protection since 2020 has changed the plant communities; and
(5) explore how these changes might shift as the climate changes in the future.

We found three separate zones in Rawdhat Khuraym. We then chose 21 study plots at random, making sure each zone was fairly represented. We surveyed the plants in the dry season and again in the wet season. In each plot we marked out three square frames, called quadrats, and recorded the plants inside each one. We also collected soil samples. To see how plant cover has changed over the years, we used satellite images and climate records.

Rawdhat Khuraym holds a rich variety of plants. In the dry season, dense trees and shrubs support the plant communities there, such as Ziziphus nummularia, Capparis decidua, Vachellia gerrardi and Capparis spinosa. In the wet season, grasses such as Cynodon dactylon and herbs such as Malva parviflora and Calendula arvensis grew strongly after the rains and took over.

We found 89 plant species from 30 plant families. Of these, 57.3% are annuals, which live for one year, and 42.4% are perennials, which live for several years. Four families stood out: the daisy family (Asteraceae), the grass family (Poaceae), the pea family (Fabaceae) and the cabbage family (Brassicaceae), which together made up 50.6% of the species. We recorded six life forms, which describe how a plant survives the dry season. Annuals were the most common, at 49.4%. Most species (55.1%) belong to the Saharo-Arabian group, which comes from the deserts of North Africa and Arabia. The next largest group (31.5%) belongs to the Irano-Turanian group, from the dry lands of Iran and Central Asia.

In the wet winter and spring, the northern part of Rawdhat Khuraym had three main plant communities. Two were dominated by the grass C. dactylon, and one by the shrub Z. nummularia. The central part also had three communities: two dominated by the herb M. parviflora and one by the herb C. arvensis. The southern part had four communities, dominated by Zilla spinosa, V. gerrardi, Rhazya stricta and C. dactylon.

As we expected, the dry summer and autumn had fewer plant communities in each part. The northern part had two (Z. nummularia, and C. spinosa with C. dactylon). The central part had one (C. spinosa with C. dactylon). The southern part had three (Z. spinosa, V. gerrardi and R. stricta).

The soil features linked to the plant communities were different in the three parts. In the northern part, the communities were positively linked with bicarbonate (HCO3), magnesium (Mg), calcium (Ca), saltiness, sulfate (SO4), clay, sodium (Na), nitrate (NO3), potassium (K), porosity (how much open space the soil has), field capacity (how much water the soil can hold after draining) and ammonium (NH4). In the central part, the communities were positively linked with silt, calcium carbonate (CaCO3) and pH (how acidic or alkaline the soil is). In the southern part, the communities were positively linked with sand and with bulk density (how tightly packed the soil is).

We compared our results with earlier studies. Five years after the area became protected, perennial plants had recovered. Most of the species we found can survive drought, and most can also cope with a moderate amount of salt.

The satellite measure of plant cover, called NDVI, showed that the northern part kept a steady plant cover of about 63% on average from 1986 to 2025. The central and southern parts had lower cover, at 38% and 40%. Changes in NDVI can be explained by how much water is available, because NDVI rose and fell together with the soil wetness index, the air's humidity and rainfall.

To predict how the plant communities will change in the future, we recommend a detailed computer modelling study. It should link changes in the plants to the environmental conditions and the climate expected in the region. This would let restoration programmes plan for future changes in the plants of Rawdhat Khuraym.

Extra material for this paper is available online at 10.1186/s12870-026-09209-y.
parts.introduction_first: Drylands cover 41% of the land on Earth, about 5.3 million square kilometres, and more than a third of the world's people live there [1]. Looking after these areas well is vital for the people who depend on them. Drylands produce little plant growth because they get little rain, are very hot, have few nutrients in the soil and have other harsh conditions [2]. Global climate change is expected to make this low growth even worse [3, 4]. That would harm the way these natural systems work, and so reduce their ability to give people the things they need [5].
parts.conclusion:
Conclusions

Our study gives an up-to-date picture of the plants in Rawdhat Khuraym. It shows that this area is a plant-rich hotspot inside a desert landscape, with 89 recorded plant species (57.3% annuals and 42.4% perennials). The main plant communities confirmed that Rawdhat Khuraym has three distinct parts, each with its own leading and important species and its own soil features.

We found that the plants in charge have shifted from sensitive annuals to tough species that can survive being trampled or damaged. This suggests that the pattern of plants is changing over time and from place to place. The links we found between plants and soil, across both space and time, support what we had noticed in the field: the plant communities are moving away from sensitive annuals and towards tough, drought-loving species such as Rhazia stricta, Capparis spinosa and Ziziphus nummularia. These patterns match what other researchers have reported in dry and fairly dry regions, where harsh conditions and human activity favour plants that are adapted to drought and can survive disturbance [71].

We also showed that water matters more than temperature in controlling which plants grow and how they change. Plants in harsh dry conditions can cope with high temperatures, but they cannot survive a shortage of water. Over the last five years, we have seen the plants recover. This could be due to more rain and to the area becoming a protected area where grazing is banned.

Our results can be used directly to protect and restore this rawdah, which matters both to local culture and to nature. For example, our list of plants can show which species are missing and should be brought back. The links we found between soil and plant communities can also help people choose the best species to plant for each type of soil. This would greatly improve how well newly planted species take root and help make restoration work better. Finally, if native plant-eating animals are to be brought back, our list of species can help judge whether a habitat is suitable in studies of whether such a project is practical.

To understand how climate change will affect the plants and restoration work, more research is needed. We need more detailed information on the small-scale effects that are predicted. We also need to combine several different satellite measures of plant cover into one model, so that we can allow for the uncertainty in predictions of how the plants will change.
parts.introduction_rest:
In dry places, plants can only survive if new young plants keep growing from seed [6]. But seedlings are under constant pressure. They face harsh non-living conditions, such as heat and drought, and living threats, such as animals that eat them. They also face gentler disturbances, such as grazing and other human activities. Together, these pressures can strongly affect whether seedlings take root in the patches of plants that grow there. This can change which plants grow and how many kinds there are [7]. In the end, many plant species may disappear from the area or move somewhere else [8].

The physical and chemical features of the soil also play an important part in shaping which plants grow. Over a long period of time, climate change together with human activities may have replaced the plant communities of the past with many different others [9, 10]. These communities could have changed from native species to tough species that can survive disturbance, and then to invasive species, which are plants brought in from elsewhere that spread quickly.

When there are no records of the past, the plant communities in natural places that have not been disturbed can act as a 'reference ecosystem'. This is a model of what the area used to be like. Whether a damaged area can recover on its own, or regrow to match this reference, depends on how badly the habitat has been damaged. It also depends on whether the ecosystem has moved into a different stable state, a new balance that is hard to change back. In some cases, people need to help the recovery along, which is called assisted regeneration [11]. This could mean adding materials to the soil to make it better, bringing back the natural flow of water, or planting missing keystone species, which are plants that many other living things depend on.

To understand what the right reference conditions are, including how the soil and the plants are linked, and to set realistic goals for restoration and protection, we need to do two things. We need to keep track of how the reference communities are changing. We also need to try restoring a target community in experiments and see how well it does as the climate changes.

The rangelands of Saudi Arabia are open lands where plants grow thinly, but they add a great deal to the variety of plants found in dry places around the world [12]. The weather in these rangelands varies, and most of them lie in the hyper-arid region, the very driest kind of climate. In fact, 32.5% of the world's hyper-arid regions are in Saudi Arabia [2]. These rangelands include many kinds of habitat, such as rawdahs. The pattern of plants in each one depends on how much moisture is available [13, 14].

A rawdah is a plant-rich catchment, a hollow where rainwater collects, and it is often described as a 'heaven of blooming flowers'. In spring, it is full of a wide variety of mesophytic plants, which are plants that like moderate amounts of water [8, 15]. People like to spend time in rawdahs for fun, for example by camping or by herding animals to graze.

Rawdhat Khuraym lies about 120 km northeast of Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, inside the Imam Abdulaziz bin Mohammed Royal Reserve, which was set up recently. One of the main goals of this protected area is to protect and increase the variety of living things and to restore damaged habitats. Rawdhat Khuraym is an important natural area that supports many different plant communities. It also matters to people's culture, because many visitors come in the winter months and it was used in the past for grazing animals.

For years, human activities have damaged this rawdah. These include off-roading, plastic litter, cutting down trees, too much grazing and hunting [16 and our own observations in the field]. As part of the country's restoration plans, soft fences were put up to keep cars out. These are rows of cement blocks placed about 1 m apart. Since the reserve was set up in 2021, visitors are not allowed to hunt, cut trees, leave rubbish, graze animals or camp overnight. Understanding how the mix of plants has changed, and why, while also thinking about the effects of climate change, will help people manage this area, which matters both to culture and to nature, based on good knowledge.

When we looked through earlier research, we found only a few studies of which plants grow in Rawdhat Khuraym and how they are arranged. In the autumn of 1993, El-Din and colleagues [17] recorded 28 plant species forming 15 plant communities. They found that soil features had a significant effect on where the plants grew and how many there were. Key soil features, such as saltiness, cations (positively charged particles such as calcium and magnesium), anions (negatively charged particles such as sulfate) and organic matter (material from dead plants and animals), were linked to more plant cover. High levels of magnesium, on the other hand, went along with less plant cover.

In the spring of 1995, Al-Farraj and colleagues [18] recorded 112 species. Most of them (90%) were annuals, and the main perennial species were Ziziphus nummularia, Vachellia tortilis and Rhazya stricta. Alfarhan [19] carried out a more detailed study of the plants of Rawdhat Khuraym from 1990 to 1999 and identified 154 plant species, mostly annuals (82%). A book about Rawdhat Khuraym, published in 2003, listed 115 plant species [20]. In the last 23 years, we could not find any published studies of which plants grow in Rawdhat Khuraym or how the vegetation is arranged.

A recent study using satellite images showed that plant cover fell significantly between 1998 and 2021. This suggests that the area is sensitive to climate change and human activities [21]. In our own earlier visits to Rawdhat Khuraym, we noticed that over the last 20 years the plant communities have shifted from sensitive annuals to tough species that can survive disturbance, such as Rhazya stricta and Capparis spinosa (these observations have not been published).

In dry places, it is essential to understand what helps restoration work. This knowledge is needed to plan good ways of protecting nature, which is a major challenge for nature, especially as living things must adapt to a changing climate [22]. To meet this challenge, protecting native species, the variety of living things and the places where species have evolved over a long time is crucial, and it should be part of any plan for protecting nature. On top of this, the stresses that build up from changes in climate, human disturbance and limited resources could make it even harder to reach restoration goals [23]. So, to design restoration and protection programmes that work, we need a thorough understanding of what these ecosystems are like and how they work.

There is a large gap in what we know about the plants of Rawdhat Khuraym, and we have seen the mix of species change. For these reasons, our study had five main aims: (1) to find out and update which plants grow in Rawdhat Khuraym and how the vegetation is arranged, in both the dry and wet seasons; (2) to find the main plant communities in each separate part of Rawdhat Khuraym; (3) to study how the plants and soil are linked, and to find which soil features control the different plant communities; (4) to judge how much the reserve's protection since 2020 has helped the plants move towards a more stable community that is adapted to stress; and (5) to explore how these changes might shift as the climate changes in the future, using records of plant cover over time. Our results could help people choose the best ways to restore and protect the area.

## Materials and methods

### Where we did the study

Rawdhat Khuraym lies about 120 km northeast of Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. It is the largest catchment inside the protected area of the Imam Abdulaziz Bin Mohammed Royal Reserve. A catchment is all the land that drains its rainwater into the same hollow. In Arabic, this catchment is called "Rawdah", and it covers about 19 km² (Fig. 1). The Dahna sand belt borders it to the east, and a rocky area full of lime (calcium carbonate) borders it to the west. The land is almost flat, sloping less than 1%, and it rises from 535 to 576 m above sea level. The soil is deep and loamy, a mix of sand, silt and clay, and it belongs to a soil type called Calciorthids-Torrifluvents [24].

Fig. 1

Map of the area we studied (Rawdhat Khuraym), showing its three ecological parts and where we placed our study plots and square frames (quadrats) in each part.

Rawdhat Khuraym is a natural hollow. In the rainy season, rainwater runs down from the higher land to the west and collects here. It is carried by several wadis, which are dry riverbeds that only flow after rain, and it leaves behind a layer of fine silt. This shape of the land creates a special natural system that supports many kinds of plants and animals, and in large numbers. The surrounding dry land has far fewer plants.

Rawdhat Khuraym sits close to two of the biggest land features of the Arabian Peninsula: the Dahna sand belt and the Nafud Desert. Both have their own typical plant communities, and this closeness suggests that the plants of the neighbouring Dahna and Nafud have affected the plants of Rawdhat Khuraym. The soil ranges from clay-rich to sand-rich. The climate is dry, with extremely hot summers, little rain and short, mild winters. The average temperature over the year is above 25°C. In summer it can go above 45°C, and in winter it stays between 10°C and 20°C. Between 70 and 100 mm of rain falls each year, during the rainy season from November to April [25].

Because water stays in the ground during the rainy season, this habitat becomes a refuge for plants and animals during droughts. In the hot summers, however, water evaporates very quickly, so much less water is held.

Based on our earlier surveys of the plants [26], we divided the area into three parts (Fig. 1):

(1) the northern part (2.78 km²), where tall shrubs of Ziziphus numularia and some Vachellia gerrardi trees dominate;
(2) the central part (2.81 km²), with low shrubs of Capparis spinosa and Calotropis procera; and
(3) the southern part (13.51 km²), with a more mixed mix of acacia trees and shrubs, and red sand creeping in from the nearby Dahna desert.

### Surveying the plants

From December 2023 to August 2024, we made field trips that covered the whole of Rawdhat Khuraym, in both the dry and the wet season. On our first visit to get to know the area, we marked out the three separate zones: the northern, central and southern parts (Fig. 1). We drew the boundaries between them by looking at differences in the shapes of the plants, the patterns of the vegetation, the shape of the land and the type of soil.

To plan the survey, we used a method called stratified random sampling [27]. This means we first split the area into groups, here our three zones, and then chose study plots at random within each group. We did this because the variety of plants, and the way the plant cover changes over distance, differ from zone to zone. Places that vary more need more sampling to give a true picture of each zone.

In total we set up twenty-one study plots across the three parts (Table S1). We placed seven plots at random in the northern part (N1 to N7), four in the central part (C1 to C4) and ten in the southern part (S1 to S10). We surveyed every plot twice: once in the wet winter and spring, and once in the dry summer and autumn. This let us see how the species changed from season to season.

In each plot, we placed three square frames (quadrats) at random, at least 500 m apart. We treated the three frames as repeats of the same measurement. We sized each frame to suit the main type of plant in the plot. For small shrubs, grasses and herbs, we used frames of 10 × 10 m (100 m²). For plots with large shrubs and trees, we used frames of 30 × 30 m (900 m²).

In each frame, Prof. Ahmed Abd-ElGawad, one of us and a professor of plant ecology, identified and recorded every plant species. He used several books on the plants of Saudi Arabia, such as those by Collenette [28], Chaudhary [29], Chaudhary [30] and Chaudhary [31], and then checked the names against the Plants of the World Online database [32].

To describe how each plant community was built up, we worked out four measurements. Density is how many plants of a species grow in a given area. Cover is the share of the ground the species covers. Frequency is how often the species turns up across the frames. Abundance is how many individual plants there are. We measured density following Bonham [33] and cover following Ellenberg and Mueller-Dombois [34].

To find out which species were dominant, we first turned the density, cover and frequency of each species in each frame into relative values, meaning each one's share of the total. We then averaged the three frames. From these we calculated the species' Importance Value Index (IVI), a single score that combines how common and widespread a species is. The higher the score, the more dominant the species. We sorted the species into life forms following Raunkiaer [35]. To find out where each species comes from in the world (its geographic group, or chorotype), we used published sources and online resources such as https://powo.science.kew.org and https://flora.org.il/en/plants/.

### Testing the soil

We took soil samples from every frame where we had surveyed the plants. In each frame, we collected three samples at random from the top 40 cm of soil and mixed them into one combined sample, following the standard method. This gave three combined samples per plot, and we tested each one separately as a repeat.

To find how much water the soil held, we used the weight-loss method: we weighed the soil, dried it, and weighed it again. We labelled the samples and took them to the Range Science Laboratory at King Saud University. There, we let them dry in the air for a set time, crushed them by hand into a fine powder, and passed them through a sieve with holes smaller than 2 mm.

We also collected three more soil samples from each frame at each site, down to 15 cm, to measure bulk density (how tightly packed the soil is). We measured the volume of soil we dug out, dried it in an oven and weighed it, following the method of Blake and Hartge [36]. From the dry bulk density, we estimated the total porosity (how much open space the soil has). For this we assumed that the soil grains themselves have a density of 2.65 g/cm³, as described by Rowell [37]. We found the soil texture, meaning how much sand, silt and clay it contains, using Bouyoucos's method [38]. We measured field capacity (how much water the soil can hold after draining) following Cassel and Nielsen [39].

We mixed one part soil with five parts water and used this liquid to measure pH (how acidic or alkaline the soil is) and electrical conductivity (EC), which shows how salty the soil is, following Blake and Hartge [36]. We measured calcium carbonate (CaCO3) with the calcimeter method [40]. We measured total nitrogen (N) with the Kjeldahl method [41] and total phosphorus (P) with the method of Nelson and Sommers [42], which uses a spectrophotometer, an instrument that measures how much light a liquid absorbs.

We measured exchangeable sodium (Na) and potassium (K), the forms of these elements that are loosely held on soil particles, with a flame photometer (PHF 80 B biologie Spectrophotometer), following Rhoades [43]. We measured calcium (Ca) and magnesium (Mg) with an atomic absorption spectrometer (A Perkin-Elmer, Model 2380, USA), following Allen et al. [44]. We measured carbonate (CO3) and bicarbonate (HCO3) with the sulphuric acid method, using titration [40]. In titration, we slowly add an acid until a reaction is complete, and the amount needed tells us how much of a substance was there. We measured chloride (Cl) by titration with silver nitrate (AgNO3) [45].

### Satellite images and satellite measures of plant cover

We used images from the Landsat and Sentinel 2 satellites to see how plant cover in Rawdhat Khuraym has changed from 1986 to 2025. To allow for differences from year to year, we used five-year periods of the satellite measure of plant cover (NDVI). This is a standard practice in satellite studies and environmental monitoring, and it matches international reporting standards [46, 47]. We calculated NDVI from Landsat 5 images for 1986 to 2000, from Landsat 7 images for 2001 to 2015 (after filling in gaps in the data), and from Sentinel 2 images for 2016 to 2025.

For each period, we chose images without clouds. For each band, meaning each colour of light the satellite records, we took the median of the pixel values, which is the middle value, so that unusual values would not throw the result off. We calculated NDVI in Google Earth Engine, an online tool for working with large numbers of satellite images, using the equation of Rouse [48]:

NDVI = (NIR − Red) / (NIR + Red)

Here, NIR is the near-infrared light and Red is the red light that the ground reflects. Healthy plants reflect a lot of near-infrared light and little red light, so this formula gives a higher value where there are more plants. For each period, we used a cut-off value of 0.18 to tell apart pixels with plants from pixels without plants. This gave us a two-class image for each period, and from it we worked out the area covered by plants, and its percentage, in each part of the study area.

### Following plant cover over time

We used Sentinel 2 images in Google Earth Engine to build a record of NDVI for each part of the study area from December 2018 to April 2025. We also downloaded monthly climate records for the study area from the NASA Prediction of Worldwide Energy Resources (POWER) data portal (https://power.larc.nasa.gov/). These records covered rainfall, air humidity, soil wetness and temperature. If any value was missing, we left that data point out.

To find which climate feature was most closely linked with NDVI, we calculated Pearson correlation coefficients. A correlation coefficient is a number between −1 and 1 that shows how closely two things rise and fall together. We did this with the Hmisc and broom packages in the R software, version 4.3.2 [49]. For each part, we also calculated the correlation between rainfall and NDVI with a time lag of 0, 1, 2 and 3 months, because plants often respond to rain after a delay.

We used time-series regression, which fits a line through the values over time, to study how plant cover has changed over the past 40 years. We set the level for statistical significance at p = 0.05. This means we called a result statistically significant when, if there were really no link or trend, a result this strong would turn up by chance alone less than 5% of the time.

### How we analysed the data

We analysed the plants in each of the three parts of the study area in both the wet winter and spring and the dry summer and autumn, to see how the mix of plants changed over time and from place to place. We put together the Importance Value Index (IVI) scores of the plant species in each part, to judge which species were dominant and which mattered most for the natural system.

We then ran a hierarchical cluster analysis on these scores, using the program JMP® Pro 16.0.0 (SAS Institute Inc.). This method groups species that have similar scores, step by step, into a tree-like diagram. It let us sort out the dominant plant communities in each part of the study area in both seasons.

To explore how the soil features relate to the mix of plants, we combined the IVI scores with the soil measurements. We then ran a one-way ordination analysis using canonical correspondence analysis (CCA) in the program MVSP, version 3.22 (Kovach Computing Services). This method arranges the plant communities and the soil features on a kind of map, so that we can see the main patterns and the environmental factors that shape which plants grow where.

To compare the plant communities and their soil features within each part of the study area, we ran a one-way ANOVA on the raw soil measurements for the winter-spring and summer-autumn seasons. ANOVA is a test that checks whether the averages of several groups differ by more than chance would explain. When it found statistically significant differences, we compared the group averages with Duncan's multiple range test, which shows which particular groups differ from each other. We ran the ANOVA in the program CoStat, version 6.311, CoHort Software, 798 Lighthouse Ave. PMB 320, Monterey, CA, USA.

Finally, we analysed the IVI scores of all the species we identified to study how the dominant and ecologically important species relate to the soil features. We used Pearson correlation to calculate a correlation coefficient (r) for each pair, and we showed these values in a heatmap, a grid of coloured squares in which the colour shows how strong each link is and whether it is positive or negative. We also used hierarchical cluster analysis to find groups of species with similar mixes and to see which sites they were linked with. We carried out all of these analyses in JMP® Pro 16.0.0 (SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC, USA).
parts.results:
## Results and discussion

### Which plants grow in Rawdhat Khuraym today

Our survey found 89 plant species in Rawdhat Khuraym. Of these, 57.3% are annuals and 42.4% are perennials (Table 1). Most annuals finish their whole life cycle during the short wet spells. This is a common strategy among desert plants, which helps them avoid the stress of long droughts [50]. The species we recorded belong to 30 plant families. Four families together held 50.6% of all the species we recorded: the daisy family (Asteraceae), the grass family (Poaceae), the pea family (Fabaceae) and the cabbage family (Brassicaceae) (Fig. S1). None of the species we recorded is listed as threatened with extinction on the IUCN Red List, the world's main list of species at risk (Table 1). Plants from these families are known for coping well with drought, and they are widely reported from dry regions of Saudi Arabia [15, 51, 52].

We also sorted the species into life forms, using the system of Raunkiaer [35]. Six life forms turned up. The most common was the annual (called a therophyte), at 49.4% of the species, followed by the chamaephyte, a low plant whose buds sit just above the ground, at 29.2%. Having many annuals is common in dry habitats [53, 54]. These annuals also have several ways to cope with harsh conditions. They can change their shape and behaviour to suit their surroundings (called phenotypic plasticity), they come in many different genetic types, and they have special ways of spreading their seeds [55, 56].

Only one of the species we recorded, Orobanche pubescens, is a parasite, a plant that gets its food from other plants.

Next, we looked at where each species comes from in the world. Scientists call this its chorotype. Of all the species we recorded, 61.8% belong to a single plant region, 33.7% belong to two regions, and 4.5% belong to several. The Saharo-Arabian group was the largest, making up 55.1% of the species. Within this group, 30.3% of all species belong to it alone, 23.6% to it and one other region, and 1.1% to it and several others (Fig. S1). This shows that the climate and soil of the study area are dominated by these conditions, and that its plants fit well with the Saharo-Arabian plant zones [57, 58]. The second largest group was the Irano-Turanian group, at 31.5% of the species. Of these, 20.2% belong to it and one other region, 6.7% to it alone, and 4.5% to it and several others.

We found 22 species with spines, meaning they have spiny stems, leaves, fruits, prickles or stipules (small leaf-like parts at the base of a leaf). Only two species, Cakile arabica and Lycium shawii, were succulents, plants with thick, fleshy parts that store water. Table 1 shows when each species flowers.

### How our results compare with earlier studies of the plants of Rawdhat Khuraym

We found three earlier published studies of the plants of Rawdhat Khuraym. El-Din and colleagues [17] described the water-related conditions that shape the plant communities of Rawdhat Khuraym in 1993. Alfarhan [19] recorded which plants grew there from 1990 to 1999. In 2003, Shalbi and Aljoloud [20] described the ecology of Rawdhat Khuraym and which plants grow together there. None of these studies gave information on which plants grow there or where they grow.

We combined the plant information from these three studies with our own results, giving a dataset of 213 plant species. It lists each species' name, family, growth form, life form, whether it resists drought and salt, and its importance to the ecosystem (Table S2).

To compare the studies, we used the importance value index (IVI). This is a score that shows how dominant a species is in a community, based on how common it is, how much ground it covers and how many species it grows with.

In all the studies, the most common growth form in Rawdhat Khuraym was the annual herb, which made up 35.0% of all species (Fig. 2A). The least common was the annual grass, at 2.7%. In 1993, perennials outnumbered annuals. In the later studies (1999 and 2003), there were fewer perennials, especially shrubs and trees. In our study, perennials have recovered. For example, the share of trees is 71.1% higher than in Alfarhan's study [19] and 16.6% higher than in the study by Shalbi and Aljoloud [20]. This trend could be due to rainfall, since average rainfall has followed the same pattern. In desert ecosystems, annual plants grow quickly after rain and finish their life cycle within a few months, so they can escape the dry periods [52, 59, 60]. We saw the same pattern in life forms when we compared the earlier studies with ours (Fig. 2B). In all four studies, the most common families in Rawdhat Khuraym were the grass family (Poaceae), the daisy family (Asteraceae), the borage family (Boraginaceae) and the pea family (Fabaceae), with small differences in which families led in each study (Fig. 2C).

As we would expect in a dry ecosystem, 87.5% of all the plants recorded in the four studies are rated as "high" or "very-high" in their ability to resist drought, while only 0.6% have low drought resistance (Fig. 3A). We saw no considerable difference between the earlier studies and ours. Most of the recorded species (61.4%) can cope with a moderate amount of salt (Fig. 3B). The soil of the study area is not salty. Its electrical conductivity, a measure of how much salt is dissolved in the soil, is 0.2–1.2 dS/m. The area is a catchment, a hollow that collects water flowing down wadis, which are dry valleys that carry water only after rain.

Most of the plants we identified in Rawdhat Khuraym (88.7%) can also cope with flooding. This shows that they are adapted to the shape of the land and to the nature of the area, which is a rawdah (Fig. 3C). After rain, water gathers in the rawdah and forms short-lived ponds. These ponds support lush plant growth and refill the groundwater [8, 54].

### Plant communities in the winter and spring

In the winter and spring, each part of Rawdhat Khuraym had its own distinct plant communities (Table 2). We found them using hierarchical cluster analysis, a method that groups communities step by step according to how similar they are. We based it on the importance value index (Fig. S2).

The northern part had three plant communities. The first was dominated by the grass Cynodon dactylon (IVI = 86.6). It grew with Ziziphus nummularia (IVI = 41.8), Vachellia gerrardi (IVI = 18.3) and Polycarpaea repens (IVI = 15.9). The second community was also dominated by Cynodon dactylon (IVI = 107.7), but this time it grew with Malva parviflora (IVI = 33.8), Calotropis procera (IVI = 25.4) and Capparis spinosa (IVI = 22.7). The third community was dominated by the shrub Ziziphus nummularia (IVI = 53.1). It grew with Vachellia gerrardi (IVI = 29.8), Polycarpaea repens (IVI = 28.4), Carthamus oxyacanthus (IVI = 33.8) and Capparis decidua (IVI = 11.7). Because Cynodon dactylon dominated two communities with different partner species, it shows that this grass has a competitive advantage and can adapt to different conditions and disturbances.

The central part of Rawdhat Khuraym also had three plant communities. Two were dominated by the annual herb Malva parviflora (IVI = 56.1 and 90.1). In one, it grew with Capparis spinosa (IVI = 47.1) and Cynodon dactylon (IVI = 47.0). In the other, it grew with Rhazya stricta (IVI = 26.7), Rumex spinosus (IVI = 23.4) and Cynodon dactylon (IVI = 12.9). The third community was dominated by the herb Calendula arvensis (IVI = 62.3), which grew with Plantago ovata (IVI = 44.0), Malva parviflora (IVI = 28.9) and Capparis spinosa (IVI = 19.0). Malva parviflora and Calendula arvensis are fast-growing annuals that use the short wet season to complete their life cycles. This strategy is widely seen among desert annual plants [61].

The southern part of Rawdhat Khuraym had the most complex plant cover, with four plant communities. The first was dominated by the sub-shrub Zilla spinosa (IVI = 61.2). Its other important species were Achillea fragrantissima (IVI = 22.7), Salvia aegyptiaca (IVI = 19.3) and Pulicaria undulata (IVI = 18.6) (Table 2). The second community was dominated by the trees of Vachellia gerrardi. It grew with the herb Convolvulus oxyphyllus and the shrubs Lycium shawii and Ziziphus nummularia. Woody shrubs like these are essential for keeping dry ecosystems stable over the long term. They help recycle nutrients, and their deep roots let water soak in and raise the amount of water under the canopy [62]. The third community was made up of Rhazya stricta, which grew with Phalaris minor, Heliotropium ramosissimum and Vachellia gerrardi. The fourth community was again dominated by the grass Cynodon dactylon, which reached an IVI of 83.5, and it grew with the trees Vachellia gerrardi and Capparis decidua.

### Plant communities in the summer and autumn

In the summer and autumn, there were fewer plant communities, because fewer annual plants were present (Table 2). The northern part had two. The first was dominated by the shrub Ziziphus nummularia, which grew with the important species Cynodon dactylon, Vachellia gerrardi and Capparis decidua. The second was dominated by Capparis spinosa and Cynodon dactylon together, with the important species Calotropis procera and the grasses Phalaris minor and Avena fatua. The shift towards a shrub-dominated community, growing alongside species that can survive disturbance such as Capparis spinosa, confirms that the pattern of plants changes with the seasons.

The central part of Rawdhat Khuraym also had two plant communities. The first was strongly dominated by Cynodon dactylon (IVI = 179). The second was dominated by Cynodon dactylon and Capparis spinosa together, and it grew with the important plants Rhazya stricta, Carthamus oxyacanthus and Pulicaria undulata.

The southern part of Rawdhat Khuraym had the same plant communities as in the winter and spring. The dominant species were the same in all three communities, which shows that perennials were the most dominant plants in the southern part all year round. The first community was still dominated by the sub-shrubs of Zilla spinosa, which grew with Pulicaria undulata, Stipellula capensis, Convolvulus pilosellifolius, Lycium shawii and Rhazya stricta. The second community was dominated by the trees of Vachellia gerrardi, which reached a high IVI of 163, and it grew with Lycium shawii, Cynodon dactylon and Ephedra ciliata. The last community was dominated by Rhazya stricta, which grew with Lycium shawii and Vachellia gerrardi (Table 2). Rhazya stricta can survive extreme stress from its surroundings because it has a special chemical defence and other adaptations [63].

### How the plants and soil are linked in the winter and spring

Table 3 shows the soil features we measured in each plant community. In the northern part, the soils of the plant communities were similar. The exceptions were soil texture, pH, nitrate (NO3) and ammonium (NH4), which varied in a statistically significant way (P < 0.05). A result is called statistically significant when, if there were really no difference, a gap this large would rarely appear by chance alone. For P < 0.05, that means less than 5% of the time.

In the central part, most soil features varied significantly between communities. The exceptions were bulk density, porosity, magnesium (Mg), bicarbonate (HCO3) and nitrate. Finally, in the southern part, the communities differed significantly in soil texture, field capacity, bulk density, porosity, pH, saltiness, sodium (Na), calcium (Ca), ammonium and available phosphorus (Table 3).

To see how the plant communities are linked to the soil, we used Canonical Correspondence Analysis (CCA). This method looks at many species and soil features at once and shows which ones tend to go together. We fed it the importance values of the dominant and important species together with the soil features (Fig. 4). The communities of each part of Rawdhat Khuraym grouped together, with very little overlap between them, which confirms that the area has distinct parts.

In the northern part, the communities were moderately linked with most soil features: bicarbonate, magnesium, calcium, saltiness, sulfate, clay, sodium, nitrate, potassium, porosity, field capacity and ammonium. In the central part, the species were linked with silt, calcium carbonate and pH. Some links were weak, as with Calotropis procera and Capparis spinosa, and some were strong, as with Calendula arvensis and Plantago ovata. In the southern part, the species were linked with the sand content and bulk density of the soil. These links ranged from weak, as with Lycium shawii, to moderate, as with Heliotropium ramosissimum, to strong, as with Zilla spinosa and Salvia aegyptica.

We also looked at species that were dominant in several communities and parts. One example is Cynodon dactylon, which dominated community 1 and community 2 in the northern part and community 4 in the southern part. It showed a strong positive link with potassium, ammonium and available phosphorus (Fig. 5 and Table S3). It showed a strong negative link with bulk density (r = -0.44). Here r is the Pearson correlation coefficient, a number from -1 to 1 that shows how closely two things rise and fall together. A positive r means they rise together, a negative r means one falls as the other rises, and values near 0 mean little link.

Like all the species in the northern part, the shrub Ziziphus nummularia, which dominated community 3 there, was positively linked with most soil features: sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium, sulfate, bicarbonate, nitrate, clay and saltiness. It showed a strong negative link with pH (r = -0.83) (Figs. 4 and 5 and Table S3). Z. nummularia has been reported as a plant that tolerates salt and drought [64]. It copes with drought by switching on genes that help it keep its water, make abscisic acid (a plant hormone that helps close leaf pores), use sugars, balance water and salts, and control harmful forms of oxygen [64, 65]. Z. nummularia has also been reported as a nurse plant, a plant that helps other plants by shaping the small patch of ground around it and by enriching the soil with nutrients [66].

In the southern part, Rhazya stricta dominated community 3. Heliotropium ramosissimum and Phalaris minor were important species in community 3. Zilla spinosa dominated community 1, and Achillea fragrantissima, Salvia aegyptiaca and Pulicaria undulata were important species in community 1. All of these species showed a strong to moderate positive link (r > 0.40) with bulk density and sand content. They showed a strong negative link with available phosphorus, sodium, calcium carbonate, field capacity and porosity (Figs. 4 and 5). This pattern shows that these species prefer sandy places with little salt [15, 52].

The trees of Vachellia gerrardi were dominant in community 2 of the southern part. They were also important species in community 1 and community 3 of the northern part, and in communities 3 and 4 of the southern part. They showed a strong positive link with bicarbonate (r = 0.46) and clay content (r = 0.45). They showed a strong negative link with calcium carbonate (r = -0.49) and ammonium (r = -0.48).

We again used CCA, this time with the soil features and the importance values of the dominant and important species together. In the summer and autumn, the second community of the northern part overlapped with the communities of the central part (Fig. 4B), while the communities of the southern part grouped apart.

Both species showed a strong negative link with pH (Fig. 5 and Table S4).

The overlap between the northern and central parts of Rawdhat Khuraym was driven by the sub-shrub Capparis spinosa, which dominated community 2 in both parts, and by the trees of Calotropis procera, which were important species in community 2 of the northern part. The grass Cynodon dactylon dominated community 3 of the northern part and communities 1 and 2 of the central part. As in the winter and spring, it showed a moderate to strong negative link with most soil features: field capacity, porosity, saltiness, sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium, sulfate, calcium carbonate, ammonium, available phosphorus, clay and silt.

### How plant cover has changed over time

The three parts of Rawdhat Khuraym showed different patterns of plant cover from 1986 to 2025 (Fig. 6). In the late 1980s, the northern part had a fairly high plant cover of 40%. This rose and then stayed steady at around 80% from the early 2000s onwards. The central and southern parts had low plant cover in the late 1980s. Cover then rose in the early 1990s in the central part and in the late 1990s in the southern part. Since the 2000s, however, plant cover in these two parts has generally fallen, possibly because of less rain. From 2006 to 2010 onwards, even though rainfall increased, the plants did not recover and cover fell further until the early 2020s (Fig. 6). Only in these last 5 years has recovery been clear. This matches the peak in rainfall and the start of the protected area, the Imam Abdulaziz bin Mohamed Royal Reserve, where grazing is banned. Figs. S3–S6 show where the plant cover was in these 5-year blocks of time.

We compared the satellite measure of plant cover (NDVI) with monthly rainfall from December 1986 to April 2025. Winter rain was very significantly linked with NDVI after a delay of one to two months (Table 5). So the plants clearly respond strongly after winter rain (Fig. S7). This could be because annual plants, which make up most of the plants, come up, and because perennials grow and flower [59]. This fits with what we found in our plant surveys.

We also looked at four climate measures: temperature, soil wetness, air humidity and rainfall (with delays). Of these, soil wetness had the strongest significant positive link with NDVI (Fig. 7). Temperature was negatively linked with all the other measures, and its strongest negative link was with air humidity. Soil wetness, on the other hand, was most strongly positively linked with rainfall, followed by air humidity and then NDVI.

The temperature in the Arabian Peninsula, the Middle East and North Africa has risen up to three times faster than the world average [67]. Under the worst-case scenario for greenhouse gas emissions (called SSP5-8.5, in which carbon dioxide emissions triple by 2075), the temperature in the Arabian Peninsula is predicted to rise by 7 °C. Rainfall is also expected to increase, with the central part of Saudi Arabia likely to get 10–40% more rain [68].

To predict future plant cover, we can use the strong link we found between NDVI and soil wetness. We worked out the numbers for a straight-line relationship, called a linear regression, using the equation NDVI = Intercept + Slope × Soil Wetness. With predictions of future soil wetness from climate models, we can now, in theory, predict how NDVI is expected to change. This could help people manage Rawdhat Khuraym.

However, the predicted rain is expected to come less often but in much heavier bursts. This could cause a lot of water to run off the surface, wash away soil and soak in poorly, leaving less water to help seeds sprout and plants grow. So the straight-line relationship between soil wetness and NDVI may not give very accurate predictions. Getting past weather records for Rawdhat Khuraym itself would possibly give more accurate results than the coarse satellite data.

NDVI is a valuable way to track changes in plant cover in dry and fairly dry areas, but it has some limits. First, the Landsat satellite images are coarse, with each pixel covering 30 m by 30 m of ground. They give a valuable long-term record, but they cannot pick out the small patches of plants typical of this dry region [69]. Second, where plants are sparse, the light reflected from the bare soil underneath can add a lot to the NDVI value [70]. Third, using a cut-off value for NDVI to decide whether plants are present can bring some uncertainty, especially in dry places with little, scattered plant cover. In a future study, other satellite measures of plant cover, such as SAVI, mSAVI and oSAVI, could be used to make the results more accurate and reduce this uncertainty.
